# MI-MIDI: Mechanistic Interpretability of Text-to-MIDI Generation Models via Probing, Lenses and Steering

- **Authors**: Jakub Poćwiardowski, Mateusz Modrzejewski
- **Venue**: cs.SD
- **Published**: 2026-08-06
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06638>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.06638v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.67

## In one line

Applies linear probing, the logit and tuned lenses, activation patching and difference-in-means steering to two public text-to-MIDI models, and shows that the architecture of the conditioning pathway determines which steering strategy stays stable.

## Problem

Mechanistic interpretability of music generation has been done almost entirely on text-to-audio models such as MusicGen; symbolic (text-to-MIDI) generators have been left out, even though the relations between notes are directly measurable in a score, which makes an intervention's effect exactly quantifiable. It is unknown what musical information text-to-MIDI models encode, where in depth their prediction is formed, and whether that information supports causal control.

## Contributions

- A mechanistic-interpretability study of text-conditioned symbolic music generation spanning probing, the logit and tuned lenses, activation patching and activation steering, which the authors state is the first centred on text-to-MIDI models.
- A comparative account of how the prediction is formed in two contrasting designs: gradual refinement across depth in a native encoder-decoder, against a sharp late rotation out of an inherited textual basis in a language model repurposed by vocabulary extension, corroborated independently by vocabulary-mass analysis, the tuned lens and activation patching.
- A bidirectional steering-evaluation protocol that runs every configuration in both orientations and decomposes the response into antisymmetric (directional) and symmetric (drift) components, yielding a specificity score that catches nonspecific layer-0 responses which a generation-volume guard alone would accept.
- An architecture-dependent intervention recipe: single-layer steering is robust in both models, while all-layer steering is stable and most specific only in the cross-attention-conditioned model and accumulates disruptively in the shared prompt-music residual stream of the decoder-only one.

## Method

Two contrasting public models are instrumented: text2midi, an encoder-decoder with a frozen Flan-T5 text encoder, cross-attention conditioning, REMI+ metrical tokenization, 18 analysed decoder layers, d=768; and MIDI-LLM, a Llama 3.2 1B decoder-only model with a MIDI-extended vocabulary, AMT absolute-time tokenization, 16 layers, d=2048. Activations are recorded in predictive alignment (the state from which token t is predicted). Four probes of the same activations follow. (1) Linear probing: one L2-regularised multinomial logistic regression per layer (C=1.0, L-BFGS, 200 iterations), deliberately low-capacity so accuracy indicates linear representation rather than probe power, with 5-fold grouped cross-validation keeping all tokens of one sequence in one fold, and a label-shuffling selectivity control. (2) Logit lens: intermediate states passed through the model's own final normalization and vocabulary projection (untied), plus a tuned lens whose per-layer affine translator is initialised to identity and distilled against the model's final distribution by KL on 60,000 held-out token positions. (3) Activation patching: prompt activations at the input to layer L are replaced with those from a contrasting instrument prompt (piano vs violin) and the shift in piano-note fraction is scored 0 (no transfer) to 1 (full), guarded by a self-patch control that is 0 by construction and a neutral-prompt control for nonspecific disruption. (4) Steering: normalised difference-in-means directions from 25 contrastive prompts per pole are added to the residual stream, either at the single source layer or at every layer. The key methodological addition is a bidirectional protocol: every configuration is run in both orientations (A-B and B-A) and the two fitted slopes are split into an antisymmetric component s_dir and a symmetric component s_non, with specificity defined as |s_dir|/(|s_dir|+|s_non|), so directional control is separated from nonspecific drift.

## Results

Probing on 1,000 generated sequences: local concepts are strongly linearly decodable in both models -- instrument family, pitch class, chord root, octave and texture density reach lifts of 0.36-0.63 in MIDI-LLM and 0.22-0.42 in text2midi (best layer: instrument family 0.940 accuracy vs 0.310 baseline in MIDI-LLM). Higher-level concepts are weak in both (chord quality lift 0.098 in each, harmonic function 0.065/0.079). Key is weak per token (lift 0.055/0.114) and much stronger mean-pooled (0.401/0.545), but the authors discount this: a pitch-class histogram control alone reaches 0.486 for text2midi -- exceeding the text2midi activation readout -- and 0.475 for MIDI-LLM, so they treat MIDI-LLM's extra 0.070 lift as suggestive rather than conclusive. On the controlled SynTheory set (N=1,080, MIDI form, mean pooling) MIDI-LLM reaches 1.000 on chord progression and 0.998 on interval; text2midi scores -0.131 lift on scale mode, which against pitch-histogram and lowest-note-relative oracles is consistent with an orderless absolute-pitch encoding. Logit lens: text2midi's agreement with the sampled token rises gradually (0.053 at layer 0 to 0.677 at layer 17), whereas MIDI-LLM stays at 0.000 through layer 8 and jumps 0.050 to 0.712 across layers 12-14. That jump is substantially a basis change, not the decision forming: the MIDI share of full-vocabulary probability mass sits near its size-based chance share of 0.30 through layer 12 and rotates to >0.999 by layer 15 in the type order special to note to time/duration, and the tuned lens makes the final prediction readable two to three layers earlier than the classic lens. Patching corroborates the same band causally: instrument transfer stays near full through layer 13 then falls to 0.62 at layer 14 and 0.27 at layer 15; the text2midi mirror experiment shows no isolated depth peak, consistent with distributed cross-attention conditioning. Steering: register and polyphony clear the exploratory |s_dir| > 2 SE rule in both models, tempo/energy only in MIDI-LLM (text2midi tempo/energy fails it at both +13.6% and -22.5%). Polyphony moves 20-40% (text2midi +39.6%/-25.7%; MIDI-LLM +21.6%/-29.8%), register only one to five semitones (+2.9%/-8.0% and +5.2%/-4.6%). The headline stability result is architecture-conditional: in MIDI-LLM single-layer injection has over fifty times less median symmetric drift than all-layer injection (0.28 vs 15.1) and all-layer injection collapses at alpha=0.75, while text2midi supports all-layer injection to alpha>=2 with the most specific directions found anywhere in the sweep (register, specificity 0.98). Norm-relative steering, which equalises the relative perturbation per layer, rules out overscaling of early layers as the cause: single-layer injection survives the full 20% range in MIDI-LLM while all-layer injection fails at 2% for tempo and 5% for register and polyphony, so the limit comes from pushing all sixteen layers together. All results are from the two released checkpoints; no hardware or human evaluation is involved, and unquantifiable attributes are offered only as audio on a demo site.

## Limitations

Stated: with one model per architecture the conditioning pathway cannot be isolated from every other design difference between text2midi and MIDI-LLM, so the steering rule is a hypothesis rather than an established architectural law. Difference-in-means directions come from text contrasts that vary lexically as well as musically, so a direction is only as clean as its contrast. The metrics are proxies -- note density stands in for tempo and energy but also rises when more notes sound together, so the tempo/energy and polyphony numbers are not fully independent. Probing labels on generations are heuristic estimates decoded from the score (key via Krumhansl-Schmuckler), so weak higher-level results may be label noise rather than absent representation. Musical concepts without an unambiguous multi-track MIDI measure are outside the quantitative protocol entirely and appear only as audio. Not stated but worth noticing: the logit-lens and patching comparison across models is confounded by unequal depth axes and by entropies taken over vocabularies of very different size (524 REMI+ tokens against 55,026 musical tokens), which the authors flag as a caution but do not correct for; steering effect sizes rest on ten seeds per point; and the strongest sequence-level probing claim is largely absorbed by a bag-of-pitch-classes control.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: A clean out-of-domain test of whether the archive's standard interpretability toolbox supports the claims usually made with it, in a setting where the output is symbolic and so an intervention's effect is measured exactly rather than judged. Three results transfer directly to how the archive should read intervention claims about reasoning. First, the paper separates a change of representational basis from the formation of a decision: MIDI-LLM's logit-lens accuracy jumps from 0.050 to 0.712 across layers 12-14, but vocabulary-mass rotation and a tuned lens show most of that jump is the readout becoming legible, not the prediction being made -- a direct caution against reading a late logit-lens jump as the moment a model decides. Second, it insists on a control that most steering work omits: a pitch-class histogram reproduces most of the sequence-level probing signal and actually exceeds the text2midi readout, so the authors decline their own strongest probing claim. That is the shape of argument the archive wants for claims that a reasoning-relevant property is 'represented'. Third, and most transferable, the bidirectional protocol gives a cheap, general test that a steering vector carries a direction rather than a disruption -- reverse it and the effect should reverse -- and quantifies the difference as an antisymmetric share; it catches layer-0 responses that shift the same way under both orientations and would pass a fluency or volume check. The stability finding is a concrete methodological warning for interpretability at large: all-layer injection was over fifty times noisier than single-layer injection in the decoder-only model and the norm-relative control shows this is the layers accumulating together rather than early layers being overdriven, so where a steering vector is injected is part of the claim being made, not an implementation detail.

## Abstract

Mechanistic interpretability of music generation has concentrated on audio models, leaving symbolic models largely unexplored. We analyze two public text-to-MIDI systems of contrasting design: the purpose-built encoder--decoder text2midi and MIDI-LLM, a Llama~3.2~1B model extended with MIDI tokens using linear probing, the logit and tuned lenses, activation patching and difference-in-means steering. Across these methods, we recover musically meaningful structure and show how architecture shapes its formation and control. Pitch, instrumentation, harmony and texture are linearly decodable in both models. text2midi refines predictions gradually across depth, whereas MIDI-LLM works largely in its inherited textual basis before a sharp late rotation into the musical vocabulary; patching identifies a matching late attenuation of prompt-driven instrument transfer. Steering produces bidirectional changes in register and polyphony in both systems, and in tempo/energy in MIDI-LLM. Our two-orientation protocol isolates directional control and shows that all-layer interventions are robust in text2midi but accumulate disruptively in MIDI-LLM. Together, the results provide a practical toolkit for tracing and controlling musical concepts in symbolic generators. Audio examples are available on a demo website.
